author: Franktradinglog
text:
The selloff continues. Next, I’m shifting from shorting beta to shorting alpha. I call it the “reverse bottleneck trade”—the counterpart to the earlier bottleneck trade.

The logic is simple: AI demand will keep growing, but that growth may slow, while upstream suppliers keep expanding capacity in response to shortages and fat margins. Once effective supply catches up with demand, bargaining power shifts back downstream. During a shortage, customers care first about availability. Good enough will do. Once supply is plentiful, they start comparing performance, cost, power consumption, and reliability again. That’s when we find out who wins orders on competitiveness and who was simply picking up overflow because the leaders couldn’t supply enough.

My watchlist includes memory runner-up MU, second- and third-tier optical players COHR and AAOI, and foundry runner-up INTC.

This trade doesn’t even require the AI bubble to burst. Supply growth just needs to start outpacing demand growth. I think there’s a very high probability these stocks put in an “Everest chart” over the next year—a towering peak followed by a collapse back down. If you don’t have the stomach to go all-in on outright shorts, anti-bottleneck pair trades are another good way to express the view: long LITE / short AAOI; long TSM / short INTC; long NVDA / short AMD or AVGO.

text:
$CRWV
 isn’t paying 15% interest. Only 4% of their debt costs that.

I went through the Q2 10-Q line by line. Out of ~$35B in debt, exactly one loan sits at 15%. It’s $1.3B, due March 2028, and already being paid down.

The 15% chart going around is the market yield on their 2032 bond. A higher yield doesn’t change what CoreWeave pays. It works like a mortgage. If you locked in at 3% and rates go to 7%, you’re still paying 3%. CoreWeave locked that bond at 9.625% and still pays 9.625%.

What they actually pay

> $6.6B of convertibles at ~2%
> ~$10B of bonds at 9-10%
> Most secured loans around 9%
> ~8.4% blended across everything

They have roughly $20B of 2026 capex left to fund, and 2027 will need more. Their main funding tool has been loans backed by customer contracts. The investment grade one backed by Meta priced around 5.9% in March. If they keep borrowing that way, I think the math holds.

Zooming out, the AI trade still looks intact to me. 
$ASML
 reported record Q3 profit this morning and said lithography demand will outrun their supply in 2027 and 2028, even after adding ~30% capacity each year. Customers are already asking about 2029 and 2030 slots. 

Demand is still outpacing supply everywhere I look.

text:
Thoughts on memory:

Anyone who thinks compute will stay in shortage while memory slides into oversupply must be smoking something. Compute and memory are destined to tighten together or deflate together. One cannot die while the other survives.

By the same logic, the pods shorting memory and going long HDD are out of their minds. How do you think HDD isn't joined at the hip with memory? You really think HDD stays safe if this cycle rolls over?

In the end, all of this comes down to nobody having conviction about what happens after 2027. Historically, we have watched P peak one to two quarters before supply ramps, then Q expands and the entire profit pool collapses. But everyone forgets that this cycle runs on nonstandard products, unlike PCs, smartphones, and general purpose servers, and that it was triggered by factors different from past cycles.

This is because of the boomers who still see memory as an industry where you make a killing in the upcycle and lose your shirt in the downcycle. These self proclaimed veterans view memory through the lens of their past experience, and since they drive the market and set the stock prices, memory trades at such a low valuation. What I keep saying is that a sharp collapse like in the past is impossible. A gradual decline is possible. But even if Samsung and SK Hynix margins were cut in half from current levels, they would still trade at a P/E in the teens. That is still roughly half of HDD valuations.

Personally, I think that as memory prices fall, other sources of demand will absorb the supply at each step down. In particular, I expect personal AI demand, led by local AI, to emerge. Looked at another way, for local AI to take off, the hyperscaler driven spike in memory prices has to be brought under control. At current memory prices, local AI can never diversify.

Just as mainframes gave way to PCs and the cloud gave way to smartphones, each time carrying the cycle from P into a Q expansion phase, I think this AI cycle will also move from frontier labs to local open source AI. Based on these historical precedents, I believe local AI will take over the memory cycle from the frontier labs and carry memory demand.

I am not saying memory prices will hold for more than a decade. Memory P will fall at some point. But what is different from the past is that new consumer devices and new consumer demand, such as open source driven local AI, will support the floor for memory.

So the market right now keeps discounting these stocks out of fear of a memory peak nobody can time. This discount is being driven by boomer investors who dismiss the idea that AI supports the downside and keep pushing the view that earnings will collapse and the trough will revert to past levels too. My point is that this is completely wrong.

$NBIS


Bloomberg Intelligence just modeled return on invested capital (ROIC) through 2030 for the clouds and neoclouds, and the 
$NBIS
 line is the one I keep staring at.

Nebius goes from roughly −6% in 2026 to about 9% by 2030. That’s the steepest climb of any neocloud in the model, and it passes CoreWeave around 2029. AWS goes the other way, sliding from ~24% to ~16% as AI depreciation piles up.

Yes, the neoclouds are still below their cost of capital in BI’s numbers. 

That’s what a buildout looks like early on: you pour the concrete and buy the GPUs first, and the returns show up after.

Nebius writes its GPUs off over 4 years, faster than CoreWeave’s 6. Meanwhile the H100 is almost four years old and still rents near 2025 prices. As Nebius’s first H100s roll off that 4-year schedule, they can keep renting with almost nothing left to depreciate, and that drops straight into margin. 

Fully written-off GPUs also shrink the capital base, so ROIC gets a lift from both sides.

If GPUs keep earning that long, the depreciation drag shrinks and that 9% moves up fast.

Bullish, but not all Neoclouds are created equal.

I'm long 
$CBRS


Cerebras is trading more than 50% below where it opened on its first day, and I just couldn’t pass up this opportunity.

UBS sees revenue going ~25x by 2030 at 46% margins, and the stock trades at about 20x 2028 earnings. 

I keep saying this: the growth story for AI is inference.

Training a model is a big upfront project. Running it, every time someone asks a question or an agent takes a step, is a bill that never stops, and the agentic shift makes that bill much bigger. A single agent task can fire off dozens of model calls, and every one of them waits on the one before it. A few seconds of waiting per call turns into minutes per task.

Cerebras attacks that wait directly. 

A GPU keeps the model’s weights in HBM next to the chip and has to pull them across for every token it generates. Cerebras builds one chip out of an entire silicon wafer, about 46,000 mm² and 4 trillion transistors against roughly 1,600 mm² and 208 billion for NVIDIA’s two-die B200, and keeps 44GB of memory on the wafer itself. 

Less waiting on memory means more tokens per second for each user, which is exactly what an agent stuck in a loop of model calls needs.

GPUs are the best general-purpose factory ever built. 

Cerebras is a specialist tool for one job, fast inference, and that’s one of the fastest-growing jobs in AI.

The stock is still richly priced and could go lower, but this is a long bet I’m willing to take.

Those contracts now cover more than 35% of revenue through 2030, with about $150B in remaining performance obligations and $32B in customer commitments, mostly cash deposits. 

Customers are paying upfront to lock in memory supply years ahead, memory has never had visibility like this.

Every HBM bit takes 3 to 4 times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, node migrations are slower and new cleanrooms take years. That keeps DRAM bit growth around the low 20s% through 2028, while AI capex, HBM content per accelerator and agentic workloads keep pushing demand higher.

The biggest knock on memory has always been the cycle. Boom, bust, repeat. Contracts like these are how you kill that argument, and Micron is clearly playing the long game here.

I was thinking about what would actually make me sell my NBIS shares. 

Simplified, these are the five things that keep me honest, with how healthy each one looks today (1 = bad / 5= good):

+ Financing gets too expensive (3/5)

NBIS still has to raise roughly $250B to build out its 5 GW, and only about 20% is secured. If converts and credit get much more expensive, or the market stops taking their paper, growth slows or the share count balloons.

+ Dilution outruns growth (4/5)

Some dilution is the price of the build-out, and I'm fine with that. What would break the thesis is ARR per share stalling while the share count keeps climbing.

+ Pricing rolls over (5/5)

The bull case leans on new contracts at $20–25M per MW and GPU prices that are still rising. If contract pricing or on-demand GPU prices start falling, the economics behind every gigawatt shrink.

+ Customers stop paying up front (4/5)

Prepayments covering 50–60% of capex tell me customers can't find this capacity elsewhere. If those shrink, demand is cooling.

+ Power slips (3/5)

Contracted power that doesn't come online on time is revenue that doesn't show up, and power is the slowest input in the whole stack.

Demand is the easy part right now. 

The weakest scores are on financing and delivery, and that's where I'll be watching.
